newsitem.title: USA: AT&T, SBC merger talks cool -- sources.
newsitem.headline: AT&T, SBC merger talks cool -- sources.

text.p: Merger talks between AT&T Corp and SBC Communications Inc have cooled, sources close to the discussions said Friday, putting on hold, perhaps permanently, what would be the largest merger in history.

The unwinding of the potential $50 billion deal is likely to refocus attention on AT&T's efforts to shore up its core long-distance business and casts a harsh light on the weakness of its efforts to enter U.S. local service markets.

Analysts said the deal -- which from the outset was given long odds of ever winning regulatory approval -- appears to have run aground in the face of unexpectedly stiff resistance from Washington regulators and widespread public criticism.

Last week, Federal Communications Commission chief Reed Hundt called the merger "unthinkable," as he sought to draw a halt to such mega-mergers in general, and the combination of AT&T and a Baby Bell local service company, specifically.

The two companies declined to comment Friday on the status of any merger talks that may have occurred between the two companies, despite AT&T Chairman Robert Allen's public campaign to win support for the idea of a Baby Bell merger.
"I don't think AT&T ever imagined that there would be such vehement opposition," said Jeffrey Kagan, an industry consultant. "They were in denial," he said.

"This was like trying to put lipstick on a rhino," agreed Scott Leland, director of brokerage Legg Mason's regulatory research group. "They were trying to dress up to make the deal presentable ... but in the past few weeks, reality set in."
Kagan, who heads Kagan Telecom Associates in Atlanta, saw AT&T's desire to pair with a regional Bell local service provider as inviting a battle with anti-trust regulators.

By contrast, the pairing of rivals MCI Communications Corp and Sprint Corp with major European partners have managed to avoid such head-on conflicts, Kagan said. "AT&T was looking for a quick fix," he said.
Cleland said he believes the impact of a failed merger will be felt largely by AT&T, not SBC, which faced a win-win situation whether or not the merger succeeded.
"It signals that AT&T wanted to rush to the end game of deregulating markets to promote wider competition, he said.

"They didn't see a good way to replicate the local loop so they wanted to buy it," Cleland said of AT&T's apparent desire to gain a foothold in SBC's seven state local phone region, which stretches from Texas to California.

While forward motion on a deal may have run into a brick wall of regulatory resistance for now, analysts said they would not foreclose future efforts by AT&T to combine with SBC or even another Baby Bell.
"We can say this deal is unravelling, but does that mean it is dead? No way," Kagan said of the AT&T-SBC talks.
"These talks between AT&T and everyone else are fluid and have been going on for years," he said. "This deal appears to be cooling down, but there is always an ebb and flow to these discussions."

"The cows are out of the barn," telecom industry cosultant Bill Bane of Mercer Consulting said of the growing trends toward consolidation in telecommunications. "It is clear that there will be mergers like this in the next few years."
Reports that the negotiations were unravelling first appeared in Friday's Wall Street Journal.
AT&T shares fell 3/8 of a point 35-3/4 and SBC was down 1/4 at 59-7/8, both in composite trading at midday Friday.
